findings.title: Slippage minOut is anchored to vault.convertToAssets, not to a fair AMM price -- AMM manipulation can hand attackers a free arbitrage on every deposit and withdrawal
findings.description: The strategy computes minOut from the ERC4626's own oracle (vault.convertToShares / convertToAssets) and applies a basis-point haircut. For sUSDe/USDe this is the staking exchange rate (~1.10), NOT the Curve AMM mid price. The Curve pool is the only entity that actually quotes USDe<->sUSDe; it can trade at any spread vs vault.convertToAssets. Because the contract uses the vault rate as its only sanity check, an attacker who moves the Curve pool away from the vault rate can drain up to (slippageToleranceBps + (curve_price - vault_price)) on every swap.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Attacker observes a pending deposit() of 1,000,000 USDe in the mempool (clients are EOAs/contracts that route through the strategy). 2. Attacker flash-loans USDe and trades to push the Curve USDe/sUSDe pool so that 1 USDe buys ~0.85 / convertToAssets sUSDe instead of the natural ~0.91. 3. Strategy computes idealShares = vault.convertToShares(1e6 USDe) ~= 909,090 sUSDe and minOut = 909,090 * (1 - bps). Even at bps=50 (0.5%) the minOut floor is ~904,545 sUSDe. The Curve pool now delivers exactly that floor (or above), satisfying the check while the attacker pockets the manipulated spread. 4. Attacker unwinds the flash loan in the same tx, profiting from the value extracted from the strategy's clients. The same attack works on withdraw, _totalWithdraw, and _withdrawFrom (all four sites use the same pattern).
findings.profitability: Profitable on any swap larger than the cost of the flash loan + Curve fees. With a 0.5% slippage tolerance, the attacker captures up to ~0.5% of the swap notional minus pool fees. For a $1M deposit that is $5,000 of pure extraction. Cost: one flash loan, two Curve trades, one EVM tx (~$50-200 of gas + flash loan fee).
findings.exploitCost: $200 in gas/fees on mainnet for a 6-7 figure profit per victim swap.
findings.affectedParties: All depositing/withdrawing clients (the swap difference is silently absorbed -- principal is decremented by REQUESTED, not RECEIVED, so the loss is socialized across the share pool and shows up as a smaller surplus/yield for everyone).
findings.rootCause: vault.convertToShares is the staking accountant of sUSDe (totalAssets/totalSupply), which is invariant to short-term market dislocations. It is NOT a price oracle for the AMM. The contract has no independent oracle (e.g., Chainlink USDe/USD) and no TWAP -- it lets the AMM grade its own homework.
findings.notes: The CLAUDE.md design fact that 'shortfall is intentionally absorbed as protocol surplus' makes the rounding-against-victim aspect by design, but it does NOT cover the case where the slippage check itself is calibrated against a non-market price. This is the primary vulnerability of the entire ERC4626MarketYieldStrategy module.

findings.title: Permanent peg loss to sUSDe is silently socialized to depositors instead of triggering pause/halt
findings.description: Withdrawal flow decrements clientBalances[holder] and totalDeposited by the REQUESTED amount, not the RECEIVED amount. Every successful withdraw therefore overstates remaining principal by the slippage gap. If sUSDe permanently depegs (e.g., Ethena bad debt), the first clients to withdraw recover ~100% of stated principal while the residual share pool is left short. Late withdrawers cannot even withdraw their full stated principal because the Curve pool no longer prices the shares high enough to satisfy the (vault.convertToAssets * (MAX_BPS - slippage)/MAX_BPS) check; their withdraws revert and they are stuck with shares that are now backed by below-par value.
findings.attackScenario: 1. sUSDe drops to $0.80 in the Curve pool (e.g., a real-world solvency event). 2. Client A withdraws 100,000 USDe of principal. The slippage check fails (vault.convertToAssets uses the staking exchange rate, which only updates as Ethena marks down totalAssets, which lags). With a generous slippage setting (~5%) the swap clears, A gets ~95,000 USDe, but clientBalances[A] is decremented by 100,000. 3. Now totalDeposited still implies a 1:1 backing that no longer exists. Client B tries to withdraw the same amount; Curve has even less depth, slippage check reverts, B's funds are stuck. 4. Even before that point, a bank run is possible: every successful withdraw makes the next one less likely to succeed because the share buffer drops faster than the principal buffer.
findings.profitability: First-mover among clients gets ~100% of stated principal; subsequent clients get nothing or are stuck. Not 'profit' per se -- it is loss reallocation. The attack does not need an attacker; it is structural.
findings.exploitCost: Zero -- this triggers naturally on a depeg.
findings.affectedParties: Late-withdrawing clients eat the entire peg loss; early withdrawers are made whole. There is no rateable, pro-rata distribution of loss.
findings.rootCause: The 'principal decremented by requested, not received' rule is documented as a positive (surplus extraction) but is asymmetric: it works only when received >= requested. When received < requested it converts a pro-rata loss into a winner-takes-all bank run.

findings.title: withdrawFrom (surplus extraction) is gated by parent balanceOf == principal, capping surplus to principal -- but more importantly the swap output bypasses surplus accounting
findings.description: Two interacting bugs in one function. (a) The parent AYieldStrategy.withdrawFrom (line 292) requires `clientBalance = this.balanceOf(token, client) >= amount`, but the child's balanceOf returns PRINCIPAL only -- so an authorized withdrawer can pull at most `min(principal, surplus)` of yield. If yield > principal, the excess yield is locked. (b) The child function checks `amount <= surplus` (uses totalBalanceOf - principal at the time of call) but then sells `convertToShares(amount)` shares and credits the recipient with whatever Curve returns. Because totalDeposited is NOT decremented, the next caller's `surplus = totalBalance - principal` is recomputed against a smaller share pool. The withdrawer can pull surplus repeatedly without triggering any per-period limit and without principal protection.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Strategy holds 1,100,000 sUSDe backing 1,000,000 USDe of client principal across multiple clients. Surplus = 100,000 USDe. 2. A compromised authorizedWithdrawer calls withdrawFrom for client A (principal=10,000, surplus share=1,000) and asks for 1,000. 3. The function calls vault.convertToShares(1,000) -- regardless of WHICH client owns the surplus, the swap drains shares pro rata. After a few such calls the share buffer is below 1,000,000 USDe of value, but principal[clients] still reads 1,000,000 USDe. 4. Now any client withdraw fails the slippage check or eats principal loss (see ECON-002). The withdrawer has effectively stolen yield from clients OTHER than client A.
findings.profitability: Equal to the entire surplus (100% extractable in one call sequence), bounded only by the parent's `clientBalance >= amount` check (which uses principal as the cap per-call but the call can be repeated across clients).
findings.exploitCost: Requires authorizedWithdrawer key. Per-call gas only.
findings.affectedParties: All clients other than the one whose `client` parameter is passed -- their pro-rata share of surplus is extracted on someone else's behalf.
findings.rootCause: The function is parameterized by 'client' but operates on shared share pool state. There is no per-client surplus accounting. Combined with the parent's principal-based cap, the function is both under-permissive (can't extract surplus > principal for one client) and over-permissive (can extract another client's surplus).

findings.title: Two-phase total withdrawal caches PRINCIPAL at Phase 1 but executes share-based pro-rata at Phase 2 -- attacker can deposit/withdraw between phases to dilute the cache
findings.description: AYieldStrategy.totalWithdrawal Phase 1 caches `state.balance = balanceOf(token, client)` -- which for this child is principal. Phase 2 calls `_totalWithdraw(token, client, withdrawAmount)`, but the child IGNORES `withdrawAmount` and computes `sharesToSell = totalShares * clientBalances[token][client] / totalDeposited[token]`. So the cached balance is used only as the eventual decrement amount (`totalDeposited -= clientStoredBalance`), while shares are computed against LIVE state. During the 24h waiting period, other clients can deposit or withdraw, changing totalShares and totalDeposited and shifting the pro rata.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Owner initiates totalWithdrawal for client A. state.balance is cached at A's principal of 100,000. 2. During the 24h window, attacker (or a colluding client) deposits 10x that amount (1,000,000) into the strategy. totalDeposited = 1,100,000, totalShares roughly +10x. 3. Owner executes Phase 2. Now sharesToSell = totalShares * 100,000 / 1,100,000 ~= totalShares / 11 -- A's pro rata is now diluted vs the moment Phase 1 was initiated. 4. The shares are sold, A is paid the diluted amount, but `totalDeposited -= 100,000` and `clientBalances[A] = 0`. The colluder then withdraws their 1,000,000, recovering their funds and leaving A short. Conversely, an attacker can _withdraw_ between phases to concentrate A's pro rata higher than expected if the goal is to grief the protocol's surplus.
findings.profitability: Direct loss to the client being totally-withdrawn equal to the price impact of intervening flow, bounded by the slippage tolerance. With a wide slippage setting and a 24h window for intervening trades, the magnitude can be 1-5% of total withdrawn balance.
findings.exploitCost: Cost of capital for 24h to inflate totalDeposited; for a stablecoin pool this is essentially the borrow rate on USDe (low, ~5% APY = 0.014% / day = ~$140 / day per $1M).
findings.affectedParties: The client being totally-withdrawn (and indirectly all remaining clients, because the underlying surplus assumption is broken).
findings.rootCause: Phase 1 caches a STALE numerator (principal at t0) that is then used as a denominator decrement at t1, while the share pro rata is recomputed at t1. Cache-and-use protocols must either freeze the entire share pool or use the cached numerator for shares too.

findings.title: First-depositor / share donation: vault.convertToAssets is independent of strategy state, but totalBalanceOf relies on totalDeposited which can be 0 with shares present
findings.description: totalBalanceOf returns 0 if `totalDeposited[token] == 0`, regardless of how many vault shares the strategy holds. An attacker who transfers sUSDe shares directly to the strategy address before any client deposit will have those shares counted into the FIRST real depositor's pro rata share -- because the very next deposit sets totalDeposited to (only) that depositor's amount, but `vault.balanceOf(address(this))` already includes the donated shares. The first depositor sees `totalBalanceOf = (donated_shares * convertToAssets) * principal / principal = donated_value`, which is then SUBJECT to surplus extraction by the authorized withdrawer.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Strategy is freshly deployed for USDe/sUSDe. totalDeposited = 0, vault.balanceOf(strategy) = 0. 2. Owner of the protocol or a malicious admin transfers (donates) 100,000 sUSDe directly to strategy. 3. First client deposits 1 USDe. totalDeposited = 1, vault.balanceOf(strategy) ~= 100,000 sUSDe + ~0.91 sUSDe from the swap. 4. totalBalanceOf for the first client returns essentially the entire donated sum, ~110,000 USDe of yield on a 1 USDe principal. 5. authorizedWithdrawer calls withdrawFrom and tries to extract this -- but is capped by parent's `balanceOf >= amount` check (1 USDe). 6. So the donation cannot be drained directly via withdrawFrom in one shot, but it CAN be drained by the donor calling totalWithdrawal on themselves: principal=0, sharesToSell=0, no extraction, BUT _withdrawFrom keeps allowing 1 unit per tx until the donor can exit. Practical impact is limited but the accounting model is wrong.
findings.profitability: Marginal in the steady state because of the parent's principal cap. Sets up confusing/incorrect totalBalanceOf reporting for downstream accounting (e.g., off-chain dashboards).
findings.exploitCost: Cost of donated tokens (must be willing to lock them temporarily).
findings.affectedParties: Off-chain accounting consumers; potentially first depositor as a setup for ECON-002.
findings.rootCause: totalBalanceOf and the share-based math do not constrain the share pool to be the result of strategy operations. There is no internal accounting of 'shares this contract minted via swaps' separate from vault.balanceOf.

findings.title: Owner can set slippage to MAX_BPS (100%) and immediately drain shares via withdrawAsOwner / withdrawFrom
findings.type: owner-controlled parameter / centralization bypass with economic impact
findings.description: setSlippageTolerance allows _bps up to MAX_BPS (10000), which means minOut = 0. The owner can therefore (a) set slippage to 100%, (b) execute withdrawAsOwner on any client (or call totalWithdrawal in Phase 2), (c) the AMM swap accepts any amount of underlying including zero, (d) the difference is silently absorbed. There is no minimum sanity (e.g., 1000 bps cap). Combined with depositAsOwner setting recipient to anyone, the owner can sandwich themselves: set slippage high, sandwich-trade Curve, run a deposit-or-withdraw, reset slippage low.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Owner observes large client principal sitting in the strategy. 2. Owner calls setSlippageTolerance(10000). 3. Owner flash-loans USDe, dumps it into the Curve USDe/sUSDe pool to push price. 4. Owner calls withdrawAsOwner(client, owner, principal). Curve pool returns far less USDe than expected -- but minOut = 0, so the swap clears. 5. Owner unwinds the flash loan; the share pool has shrunk by the manipulated amount, but principal is decremented only by `amount`. 6. Owner calls setSlippageTolerance(50) to cover tracks. The next legitimate withdraw fails (or succeeds with massive loss for the next client).
findings.profitability: Up to 100% of any client's principal (limited only by Curve pool depth and the owner's flash loan capital).
findings.exploitCost: Owner key + a few gas. This is a centralization risk but C4 explicitly notes 'unintended privilege' is in scope -- here the privilege to set slippage to 100% likely was not intended (the constant MAX_BPS suggests a sanity bound, but the require uses <=, not <).
findings.affectedParties: All clients with principal in the strategy.
findings.rootCause: Bound check `_bps <= MAX_BPS` should be `_bps <= REASONABLE_MAX (e.g., 1000 = 10%)`. There is also no timelock on slippage changes.

findings.title: setRoute is owner-callable with no timelock and immediately mutates the swap path -- owner can front-run a deposit by routing through a malicious pool
findings.description: The adapter validates that path[0] == tokenIn and path[last_nonzero] == tokenOut, but does NOT validate the intermediate pools. Curve Router NG accepts arbitrary pool addresses for each hop. The owner can install a route through a pool they control (e.g., a fresh, owner-funded Curve pool with 99% slippage on every trade), then call any deposit/withdraw flow on the strategy. The strategy's slippage check uses vault.convertToAssets, not the new route's price, so the swap clears with massive value loss to the strategy.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Owner deploys a custom Curve-compatible pool C-mal where USDe trades 1:0.0001 sUSDe. 2. Owner calls setRoute(USDe, sUSDe, [USDe, C-mal, sUSDe, 0,0,...], ...). 3. Owner calls strategy.depositAsOwner(USDe, 1,000,000, owner). The strategy sends 1M USDe to the adapter, which routes through C-mal, getting 100 sUSDe back. The slippage check passes only because (1M USDe / vault rate) * (1 - bps) is ~909,090 -- ECON-001 says this check is broken. 4. With slippage = 10000 (ECON-006), the check is bypassed entirely; with slippage at any value the route through a malicious pool is not pricetested. 5. Strategy's share pool drops from 909K sUSDe to 100 sUSDe; clientBalances[owner] = 1M USDe (real obligations to other clients are unaffected on paper but the share buffer is gone).
findings.profitability: Up to the entire share pool value per call.
findings.exploitCost: Cost of deploying a malicious Curve pool (~$50-100) + gas. Owner key required.
findings.rootCause: Route mutability is not gated by a timelock or off-chain attestation. Intermediate pool addresses are not whitelisted. Combined with owner-controlled slippage, this gives the owner a one-tx drain. Audit-grade mitigation: timelock setRoute by 24h+, or ban setRoute after initial setup, or whitelist pools.

findings.title: CurveAMMAdapter does not refund residual approval after a failed swap mid-revert -- and there is no leftover balance sweep
findings.description: swap pulls amountIn from msg.sender and forceApprove(router, amountIn). If router.exchange consumes less than amountIn (Curve Router NG generally consumes everything but partial-fill behavior is pool-type dependent), the remaining approval persists. There is no refund of residual tokenIn back to msg.sender either, so any unused tokens remain stranded in the adapter. Over time the adapter accumulates dust the strategy paid for but never sees -- this dust is socialized away from clients.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Strategy calls adapter.swap with amountIn = 100,000 USDe. 2. Curve pool absorbs only 99,999 (rounding or pool internal dust). 3. 1 wei stays in the adapter; the strategy decremented its on-chain balance by 100,000 but only got value for 99,999. 4. Across many calls this accumulates. The adapter has no sweep function and no refund-to-caller path; the residue is permanently stranded.
findings.profitability: Tiny per-call. Compounds over time. Not directly exploitable.
findings.rootCause: Missing post-swap balance check + refund. Standard AMM-adapter pattern is `transfer back any residual tokenIn to msg.sender`.

findings.title: Curve Router NG sUSDe pool exposed to read-only reentrancy via meta-pool token lookups
findings.description: The Curve sUSDe-USDe route in AMMRoutes.json (pools 0xF55B0f6F2Da5ffDDb104b58a60F2862745960442 and 0x57064F49Ad7123C92560882a45518374ad982e85) is a 2-hop path through Curve crypto-pools (swap_type=1, pool_type=10). Curve crypto pools have a documented read-only reentrancy bug whereby calls to get_virtual_price during a remove_liquidity call return stale values. The strategy DOES NOT call get_virtual_price directly, but it DOES call vault.convertToAssets/convertToShares before the swap and the strategy's totalBalanceOf is called by external clients via downstream contracts. If any client holds a position whose accounting reads totalBalanceOf during a Curve callback, stale share count + stale principal == accounting drift.
findings.attackScenario: Requires (a) Curve pool callback into a contract that reads strategy.totalBalanceOf, and (b) timing the read between strategy's swap call and Curve's state finalization. Not directly exploitable in the in-scope code today because totalBalanceOf is view, but this is a footgun for any future client contract (e.g., a Vault that mints LP shares based on totalBalanceOf -- the standard Curator pattern).
findings.profitability: Depends on downstream consumers. None visible in scope.
findings.exploitCost: Curve crypto-pool reentrancy is well-documented; flash loan + 1 tx.
findings.affectedParties: Downstream consumers of totalBalanceOf, if any are reentered into during a swap.
findings.rootCause: No reentrancy lock around the swap path that protects view readers. The strategy's nonReentrant guard protects only itself, not external observers.
findings.notes: This is a forward-looking concern; in the current scope no contract exists that reads totalBalanceOf during a Curve callback. Document for future client integrations.

findings.title: Sandwich economics: every public deposit/withdraw is profitable to sandwich because slippage tolerance is global
findings.description: Slippage is owner-set globally and not per-call. A client cannot override it. Therefore for any swap larger than the slippage budget * pool depth, sandwich profit = (slippage * tradeSize) - gas - flash loan fees. With Curve's Router NG, the path 'USDe -> Curve(USDe/USDC) -> Curve(USDe/sUSDe) -> sUSDe' has thin USDe/USDC depth. A 100K USDe deposit with 50bps slippage is sandwich-profitable at the level of $250-500 per call.
findings.attackScenario: Standard sandwich: front-run with tokenIn, let victim trade, back-run with tokenOut. Profit ~ slippage_bps * notional - fees. For a 0.5% tolerance and $100K trade -> $500 captured by MEV.
findings.profitability: 0.1-1% of notional per swap, depending on pool depth.
findings.exploitCost: Standard MEV bot infrastructure, ~$0 marginal cost per trade.
findings.affectedParties: Whichever clients call deposit/withdraw -- the loss is socialized into the share pool.
findings.rootCause: No per-call minOut override; no commit-reveal; no batch auction; no use of Curve's get_dy as a tighter sanity check immediately before the swap.

findings.title: convertToShares-based minOut breaks if sUSDe share price drops (Ethena slash / liquidation event)
findings.description: The contract banner says 'Rebasing vaults are NOT supported. This strategy assumes vault share prices only increase (or stay flat) over time.' But sUSDe IS subject to slashing / loss events: if Ethena's hedge legs go badly and totalAssets drops, convertToAssets(shares) drops too. The contract's slippage check then becomes LOOSER (allows worse prices on withdraw), which means client withdrawals lose value silently rather than reverting.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Ethena marks down totalAssets by 5% due to a hedge loss. 2. Existing client A calls withdraw(100,000). 3. sharesToSell = convertToShares(100,000) returns more shares than before (because each share is worth less). 4. minOut = idealUnderlying * (1 - bps) -- but idealUnderlying is now lower, so minOut is also lower. 5. The swap clears at the new lower price; client A receives 95,000 USDe but clientBalances[A] decrements by 100,000. 6. The 5,000 loss is silently absorbed and shows up as principal drift (see ECON-002).
findings.profitability: Loss to clients equal to the magnitude of any share-price drop.
findings.exploitCost: Zero -- happens on any real Ethena loss event.
findings.affectedParties: All clients with principal at the time of the drop.
findings.rootCause: The strategy treats convertToShares/convertToAssets as a sticky reference even though it is precisely the value being protected. It should additionally enforce a 'price-floor' relative to the previous deposit's share price OR pause on any decrease.

findings.title: _emergencyWithdraw transfers raw vault shares to owner, allowing owner to bypass two-phase withdrawal protections entirely
findings.description: AYieldStrategy.totalWithdrawal enforces a 24h waiting period explicitly 'to provide community protection against rugpulls'. _emergencyWithdraw bypasses this entirely: it is owner-only, has no waiting period, and transfers raw sUSDe shares directly to owner. The owner can call emergencyWithdraw(allShares) and walk away with the entire share pool in one tx, defeating the rugpull protection.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Owner calls emergencyWithdraw(type(uint256).max). 2. _emergencyWithdraw caps at totalShares and transfers all sUSDe directly to owner(). 3. Strategy now holds 0 shares; client withdraw calls revert because sharesToSell > availableShares=0 falls through cap and causes downstream swap failure. 4. clientBalances are not zeroed, so on-chain accounting still shows clients owning principal that doesn't exist.
findings.profitability: 100% of the share pool to a malicious owner.
findings.rootCause: The two-phase withdrawal is the documented safety mechanism, but emergencyWithdraw provides a parallel zero-delay path. Either emergencyWithdraw should also be subject to the two-phase delay, or it should be removed (totalWithdrawal already covers the legitimate emergency case).
findings.notes: Pure-centralization risks are typically out of scope for C4 bounties, but the documentation explicitly markets the two-phase delay as a safety property. Bypassing a stated safety property is in scope per C4 'spec deviation' rules.

findings.title: convertToAssets/convertToShares-based minOut creates round-trip arbitrage between deposit and withdraw within the same block
findings.description: Both deposit and withdraw use vault.convertToShares/convertToAssets, which is invariant within a block (changes only when sUSDe accrues yield via a vesting drip). An attacker who is an authorized client can deposit X USDe (gets `idealShares - dust`), immediately withdraw X USDe (sells `convertToShares(X)` shares = the same `idealShares`), receives `convertToAssets(idealShares)` USDe back. If the Curve pool is below the convertToAssets midpoint (very common -- Curve fees alone make this true) the round trip is profitable to the strategy by the spread, BUT the principal accounting decrements by REQUESTED. If the round-trip nets a slippage shortfall the attacker who is an authorized client can WALK AWAY with most of their principal still credited and have eaten 0.5% (slippage) of OTHER clients' surplus.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Authorized client A deposits 1,000,000 USDe. clientBalances[A] += 1M. Strategy's share pool +909,090 sUSDe minus pool fees. 2. A immediately withdraws 1,000,000 USDe. The strategy sells 909,090 sUSDe back, receives ~999,000 USDe (after Curve fees), pays A 999,000, clientBalances[A] -= 1,000,000 (back to original). 3. Net: A has lost 1,000 USDe of REAL value but its on-chain principal balance is unchanged. From the strategy's view, totalDeposited dropped by 1,000,000 even though the share pool is now short. 4. Other clients experience a smaller share pool with the same totalDeposited -- their surplus is now negative or zero, and any subsequent withdraw eats the loss. A has effectively griefed other clients into eating their fee.
findings.profitability: A loses money in absolute terms but the loss is socialized away from A's principal balance. Profitable as a griefing attack against a competing client; not profitable for the attacker individually unless A is being paid externally to do this.
findings.exploitCost: Cost of Curve fees on a round trip + gas. ~$50-200 per million notional.
findings.affectedParties: All clients other than the round-tripper.
findings.rootCause: The 'principal decrements by requested, not received' rule has an inverse failure mode for round trips: deposit credits principal at face value, withdraw debits principal at face value, but the share pool absorbs both rounds of slippage.

findings.title: Cross-client share-pool mixing: client A's withdraw uses TOTAL shares as the 'available shares' cap, not their proportional shares
findings.description: When client A withdraws, sharesToSell is computed as convertToShares(amount) and then capped to vault.balanceOf(address(this)) -- the TOTAL share pool. There is no proportional cap. If client A's principal is 100,000 but the share pool also contains client B's 1,000,000, A can withdraw up to A's principal (100,000) using shares whose value > 100,000 USDe (because the AMM may overprice them, or A's principal could be inflated by past donations). More practically: if the share pool shrinks below the implied value of remaining principal (e.g., after a depeg), A's withdraw drains UP TO A's stated principal worth of shares, leaving B short. A is paid in full; B is paid nothing.
findings.attackScenario: 1. Strategy holds 1.0M USDe-equivalent share pool, principal split A=500K, B=500K. 2. sUSDe drops 10% in the AMM. Share pool now ~900K USDe-equivalent. 3. A calls withdraw(500,000). sharesToSell = convertToShares(500,000). The slippage check uses convertToAssets and lets the swap clear (with a 5% tolerance and a 10% drop, it actually reverts; with a 15% tolerance it clears). A receives ~450,000 USDe, clientBalances[A] -= 500,000 = 0. 4. Share pool is now ~450K USDe-equivalent backing 500K of principal still owed to B. B's withdraw will revert or eat all the loss.
findings.profitability: Equivalent to ECON-002 -- structural rather than 'profitable' to the attacker. But the asymmetry between A's outcome and B's outcome IS the loss vector.
findings.exploitCost: Zero -- triggers naturally on any depeg or sustained sandwich attack.
findings.rootCause: No proportional cap. A's withdraw should be capped by `(clientBalances[A] / totalDeposited) * totalShares` shares, not by total shares. This would convert the loss from winner-takes-all to pro rata.

findings.title: AMMRoutes.json USDe<->sUSDe path uses two cryptopools but only USDe<->USDC<->sUSDe ordering -- a route addressing single-pool sUSDe/USDe Curve directly is not used
findings.description: The configured route is USDe -> 0xF55B... (USDe/USDC pool) -> 0xf939E0A0 (USDC token, intermediate) -> 0x57064F49... (sUSDe/USDC pool) -> sUSDe. This is a 2-hop route through USDC, paying Curve fees twice. There exists a direct sUSDe/USDe Curve pool (not configured here). The 2-hop route exposes the strategy to USDC depeg risk in addition to sUSDe peg risk -- if USDC depegs even briefly, both legs of the swap suffer.
findings.attackScenario: 1. USDC depegs to 0.98 for 30 minutes (CB-related event). 2. Strategy executes a deposit; first leg trades USDe -> USDC at favorable rate (USDC undervalued). 3. Second leg trades USDC -> sUSDe at unfavorable rate (USDC undervalued). 4. Net result is approximately neutral but exposed an extra hop's slippage tolerance. Worse: an attacker can sandwich BOTH pools simultaneously.
findings.profitability: Marginal under normal conditions; significant during USDC depeg events.
findings.rootCause: Route choice should be a single-pool sUSDe/USDe path, not a multi-hop USDC-routed path. Verify against Curve's direct sUSDe/USDe pool address.
findings.notes: Configuration issue, not contract code. May be intentional if direct pool has insufficient liquidity.
